doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
title: Bands seen at the Oakland Auditorium and Kershner Gardens
summary: Wartime promoters move the black bands to Oakland Auditorium; he saw Kirk, Fields, Lunceford, Sissle and Ellington as a record-collecting teenager.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Same band. When Lunceford’s band came through, white night, colored night. Basie’s band came through, white night, colored night. Glenn Miller band came through, white night, colored night. Louis came through with a group, colored night, white night. Fats Waller, colored night and a white night. But then when the war came, suddenly the population increased and people were working 24 hours a day in three 8-hour shifts. So people had plenty of money and they could go out and they didn’t mind, see, if you had to leave the dance early to go to work. But what happened, it expanded so and Sweet’s, with a 2,500 person capacity, they couldn’t handle the crowds. So Sweet’s turned over the colored bands to a fella named John Burton, lived in Berkeley. And John became a promoter. And so then they started using the Oakland auditorium. And so then the bands would come to the Oakland auditorium. And they would draw. They would draw, like I say, Hampton, he’d draw 7,500 people, Basie over 5,000, Nat King Cole came in with just four people — the place was packed. Then I saw — who else did I see there at the Oakland auditorium during the war. See the USO shows would come here. And many of them had bands from back east with them. So that took care of the transportation costs. So when the show got out here, the bands then, the different promoters would book them up and down the coast. And I would go to the Oakland auditorium every time a big band would show up, I’d be right there. Because when I was a teenager I collected records. And so I would have all these different records of these different Eastern bands, and this was my chance to see them in person. So I saw the Andy Kirk band, and you know Pha Terrell, the singer, they were — oh man, they were a top flight band. I saw another band at the Kershner Gardens, which later became the Alabama, I saw the Ernie Fields band out of Oklahoma, they were one of the well-known territory bands. Then at Sweet’s of course, as I mentioned before, I saw Lunceford and Louis and all those fellas, as well as Glenn Miller. Then at the Oakland auditorium the Carolina Cotton Pickers — they may be named somewhere, I’ve seen their name somewhere in one of the books on big bands. The Carolina Cotton Pickers, as I mentioned before, the Andy Kirk band with Mary Lou Williams, she was playing piano at the time. And Ed Thigpen’s father, Vin Thigpen, he was the drummer in the band. And Dick Williams, the tenor player, he and Mary Lou Williams were married. And the guy — he and Eubie Blake—
Noble Sissle’s band. I can’t always — oh yeah, they were in their tuxes and everything. And of course the Duke’s band. I saw the Duke’s band at the auditorium.
